finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> deletes any file without an authorization check because the result of require_allowed (is_allowed) is discarded instead of enforced.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid>; no identity or grant is required.

trace.note: DELETE /files/<fid> route registered with no auth decorator or guard
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') called; boolean return value discarded
is_allowed returns a bool and never raises or aborts
file deleted regardless of the authorization result

finding.guards_checked: load_user (views.py:10-12) only assigns g.user from a header and enforces nothing; is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is non-enforcing; no route decorator, middleware, or blueprint guard. Sibling rename_file uses ensure_allowed (views.py:26), which aborts 403, so the DELETE route used the wrong variant.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user from a request header and enforces nothing. The route at views.py:15 has no auth decorator. is_allowed, imported as require_allowed (views.py:4), returns a bool (acl.py:5) and the call at views.py:18 is a bare statement whose result is discarded. Only ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, which aborts 403) would enforce, and the DELETE route does not use it. The sibling rename route at views.py:26 does use ensure_allowed.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at views.py:18 calls require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4-5), which returns a bool that is never tested, so views.py:19 deletes the file for any caller, including an anonymous one with no X-Session-User-Verified header, since load_user (views.py:12) enforces nothing.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header without verification, allowing impersonation of any user with grants.
finding.source: X-Session-User-Verified request header, set freely by any client when the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that strips and rewrites it.
finding.sink: g.user used as the principal for authorization at views.py:18 and views.py:26, with grant lookup at acl.py:5

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no signature, session lookup, or source check
g.user passed to is_allowed in delete_file
g.user passed to ensure_allowed in rename_file
grants keyed by attacker-chosen user value

finding.guards_checked: No cryptographic verification of the header; no check that the request came from a trusted upstream; absent header yields grants.get(None, []) which is empty unless data contains a None key. The header name implies an upstream check that is not present in this code. Severity depends on deployment; flagged for explicit security review because it weakens authentication.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed at acl.py:8-10 (raises abort(403) on failure) guards rename_file at views.py:26, but it keys on the spoofable g.user, so it does not stop impersonation. At views.py:18, require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) is a bare statement whose bool return is discarded, so it is no guard at all. Deployment-level proxy stripping of the header is not present in this code and cannot be verified here.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the request header with no verification, and views.py:26 with acl.py:8-10 authorizes rename against that value, so any client that can reach the app can impersonate a user with grants (the trace's delete path at views.py:18 is worse: is_allowed's result is discarded, so delete_file has no authorization at all).

finding.claim: Unhandled KeyError for a missing file ID returns HTTP 500 while an existing but unauthorized ID returns 403, letting a client distinguish existing IDs (existence oracle). Low severity.
finding.source: Any client that can guess or enumerate fid values.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup in delete_file (views.py:17) and rename_file (views.py:25)

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for a nonexistent ID, producing a 500
existing ID without write grant yields 403 via ensure_allowed

finding.guards_checked: No STORE.get with a 404 response. Impact is limited to ID enumeration and only matters if IDs are guessable.

verdict.guard_found: For rename_file, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 on failure and views.py:26 calls it as a statement, so it is effective. For delete_file, require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) returns a bool that views.py:18 discards, so it is not a guard at all.
verdict.reason: The 500-vs-403 oracle only exists for rename (views.py:25-26); in delete_file, views.py:18 calls require_allowed as a bare statement, so is_allowed's bool (acl.py:5) is discarded and an existing ID with no grant is deleted with 200 (views.py:19-20), not 403, so the trace's claim is wrong and the real defect is a missing authorization check on DELETE, which is a more serious issue than the low-severity oracle the candidate describes.
